Nearly 200 days into the war between Washington and Tehran, developments continue on multiple fronts.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iran is "in a state of war," describing the ongoing naval and economic blockade as an act of aggression. He stressed that Tehran’s measures to counter the blockade are defensive and in accordance with international law. He also underscored the importance of diplomacy, but said negotiations would not be possible unless the other side is willing to engage.

Amid diplomatic efforts, Tehran announced that a meeting is expected to take place in Muscat on Monday, bringing together Iran, Iraq and Gulf states to discuss the outcome of Iranian-Omani talks aimed at establishing safe routes for navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, US Central Command said it has diverted the routes of 99 commercial vessels since the blockade of Iran began. # Iranian official says US, Israeli attacks prompted denial of IAEA access



US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities were the main reason Tehran refused to grant the International Atomic Energy Agency access to some sites, a Foreign Ministry official said on Sunday.

Hossein Noushabadi, the ministry’s director-general for parliamentary affairs, said the UN nuclear watchdog should have acknowledged that explanation in its report.

He described the IAEA Board of Governors resolution against Iran, proposed by the United States and three European countries, as legally invalid and contrary to the agency’s mandate.

# Iran Will Meet With Gulf Arab States as Mideast Conflict Widens

Talks are expected tomorrow, officials said. Diplomacy to end the war with the United States has stalled and Iranian-allied forces have advanced in Yemen.

Iranian officials will meet on Monday in Oman with representatives of some of the Gulf Arab states that it has repeatedly attacked during its war with the United States and Israel, as the regional conflict has widened in recent days.

Yemen has emerged as the latest front in the fighting, with the Iranian-backed Houthi militants there seizing the strategic port of Mokha and the island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea last week. They have also attacked Saudi energy sites and sought to blockade Saudi shipping, exacerbating a global oil and gas crisis prompted by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West Pipeline on Friday after it was targeted by drones from Iraq. That pipeline has been a critical lifeline for the country’s oil exports after Iran effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. No one took responsibility for the drone attack, but Iraq has long harbored well-armed militias backed by Iran.

# PM's top security adviser says Europe faces hard winter to keep pressure on Putin

![National Security Adviser of the United Kingdom Jonathan Powell is pictured outside 10 Downing Street in October 2025.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/6aea/live/e1c6da50-af0c-11f1-b7ba-f9c30afb9e4d.jpg)

**The UK national security adviser has said Europe must be ready to endure "real hardship" this winter if it is to keep up economic pressure on Russia.**

In rare public remarks, Jonathan Powell told a conference in Kyiv that Europe's strategy of supporting Ukraine and imposing sanctions on Moscow was working.

Powell said talk of Russian escalation was "not a problem" but a "sign of success" that pressure on President Vladimir Putin was finally paying off - and as such European nations should not take their "foot off the gas".

His optimistic remarks come as Russia continues to target Ukrainian infrastructure and as Europe faces a severe energy shortage this winter after drastically reducing its dependence on Russian oil and gas.

Despite Russia's full-scale invasion now being in its fifth year, Powell said Ukraine had "already won" because Putin would not be able to seize the whole country and "a free Ukraine in Europe" would be able to choose its own direction regardless of any territorial loss.

The prime minister's most senior security adviser was in Ukraine's capital only last weekend for talks with US President Donald Trump's envoys after they visited Putin in M

# Trade wars are going electric. The planet could pay the price.

Tariffs on everything from EVs to grid components could slow the energy transition.

09/13/2026 04:00 PM EDT

BRUSSELS — Import limits on solar technology. Export controls on critical minerals. Rising tariffs on photovoltaic cells, electric vehicles and batteries.

The list of trade barriers grows every day, in countries around the world, ensnaring an electrification supply chain that is crucial to slashing global fossil fuel use, meeting rising power demand and staunching the rise of electricity bills.

Governments from Brussels to Brasilia, craving a slice of the booming clean economy and eager to counter China’s green technology dominance, have turned to a range of trade measures in an effort to secure jobs and protect domestic manufacturing. Meanwhile, the United States has not only unleashed a wave of tariffs across the board under President Donald Trump but also issued more targeted levies on Chinese solar products and grid imports.

The result could be a slower global energy transition, more planet-warming emissions and a hotter climate.

“It is slowing things down for sure,” said Karen Wayland, CEO of the GridWise Alliance, a coalition of U.S. electric utilities, equipment makers and technology providers focused on grid infrastructure.

Industry, utilities and analysts are warning that rising trade barriers threaten to stifle electrification and make the switch to cleaner energy more expensive.

Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly taking the wheel in designing China’s next-generation semiconductors, as Beijing and domestic technology firms accelerate efforts to integrate AI into chip design software to bolster national self-sufficiency.

Empyrean Technology, China’s top maker of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, has been accelerating the chip design process by using AI-optimised algorithms and agentic tools, according to company chairman Liu Weiping.

By applying an AI agent to its simulation and layout tools, the company slashed the time needed for a circuit layout task from four weeks to just one week, Liu said.
